site.name: atlas-tutor
site.summary: atlas-tutor Fictional AI math & CS tutor "Atlas Tutor" chat fixture. UXBench fixture in the Chatbot / Agent Interface category. Layout **Three-column desktop:** - **Left rail (260 px)** — branded sidebar with New-chat button, search, Subjects nav (Mathematics / Programming / Physics / Statistics / Linear algebra with counts), and threaded history grouped by recency (Today / Last 7 days / Earlier — 11 threads total). Sticky profile-mini footer with streak badge. - **Center (flex)** — conversation viewport with sticky head ("Chain rule — when both functions move" · model · last reply · 3 head-tools); messages area centered to 820 px; sticky composer at the bottom with attach / textarea (Cmd+Enter to send) / mic / send-button row plus suggestion chips and a model selector. - **Right rail (320 px)** — practice problems panel (6 chain-rule problems with difficulty pills / hint button / 3-state Solve→Submit→Correct toggle), Concepts card (4 internal links), Your progress card with progress bar updated as practice is completed. Conversation pre-fill

run_plan.goal: Explore the Atlas Tutor interface to validate the primary chat flow, the right-rail practice problem interaction, and the settings/privacy configuration (triggered by the gear icon), while identifying mobile usability issues.
run_plan.summary: The run will proceed in three phases: first validating the core chat and navigation interactions; second, exercising the 'Practice Problems' panel state machine (Solve -> Submit -> Correct); and third, accessing the Settings modal via the profile gear icon to check privacy controls. The exploration will conclude with a mobile viewport pass to verify layout responsiveness against the known tap-target risks.
assumptions: The site is a Single Page Application (SPA) where 'Settings' opens as a modal or overlay rather than navigating to a new URL.
The 'Practice' panel on the right rail functions independently of the main chat stream.
The '⚙' icon in the bottom-left profile footer is the entry point for the requested settings/privacy flow.
risk_hotspots: Profile Footer Gear Icon (ux-4): Small tap target (22x21px) likely difficult to hit on mobile.
Right Rail Practice Panel: State transitions (Solve/Submit/Correct) need validation for visual feedback.
Composer Area: Attachment and Mic buttons proximity to the text input on narrow viewports.

phases.title: Core Chat & Navigation Validation

Verified composer input field accepts text and triggers UI state changes.

phases.title: Practice Problem Interaction Flow
phases.objective: Validate the state machine of the Right Rail practice problems (Solve → Hint → Submit).
key_checks: Select a problem from the Right Rail (e.g., Problem #1 'd/dx sin(3x + 2)').
Click 'Hint' to verify tooltip or text expansion.
Simulate solving: Click 'Solve' (or type answer if input appears) and then 'Submit'.
Verify the 'Correct/Incorrect' feedback state updates visually.
Check if the 'Your progress' card updates after completion.
exit_criteria: Successfully completed one full cycle of a practice problem.
Observed visual feedback for both 'Hint' and 'Submission' states.

phases.title: Settings & Privacy Configuration
phases.objective: Access the settings menu via the profile footer and inspect privacy/data controls.
key_checks: Locate and click the Gear icon (ux-4) in the bottom-left profile footer.
Identify the resulting modal or drawer.
Toggle any available privacy switches (e.g., 'Share data for training').
Close the settings modal and verify return to main chat state.
exit_criteria: Settings modal successfully opened and closed.
At least one privacy-related control identified and interacted with.

phases.title: Mobile Responsiveness & Risk Check
phases.objective: Repeat critical checks on mobile viewport to confirm layout warnings and tap targets.
key_checks: Switch to mobile viewport (e.g., iPhone SE or Pixel 5).
Verify if the Left and Right rails collapse into hamburger menus or drawers.
Attempt to tap the Profile Gear icon (ux-4) to check for mis-hit risks.
Verify the Composer (ux-25) does not overlap with the keyboard or header.
Check if 'Practice' panel content is accessible or hidden on mobile.
exit_criteria: Confirmed behavior of sidebars on mobile (hidden vs. stacked).
Documented any unreachable controls due to screen real estate.

observation.title: Atlas Tutor — math & CS tutor
observation.visible_text: Atlas Tutor + New chat 🔍 SUBJECTS 𝒙 Mathematics 12 {} Programming 7 ⚛ Physics 3 ∮ Statistics 4 ∇ Linear algebra 5 TODAY Chain rule — when both functions move Big-O of recursive Fibonacci L'Hôpital's rule — when can we apply it? LAST 7 DAYS Eigenvalues of a 3 × 3 matrix Bayes' theorem — disease testing Binary search — off-by-one bugs Why does e^x derive to itself? Markov chain steady state EARLIER Proof by induction — sum 1..n Tail recursion vs. loop Series convergence tests cheatsheet Probability of repeat birthdays SA Selene Aiyer Atlas Plus · 14 days streak ⚙ Chain rule — when both functions move Calculus · single variable · last reply 12:08 PT · Atlas-3 model ⌥ Steps ▶ Practice ⋯ SA I keep getting tangled up when I have to differentiate sin(x²). Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! Try this kind of unpacking on the practice problems in the right pane — start with #1. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Can you also write a tiny Python helper that prints the derivative for me using sympy, so I can sanity-check my work? A Sure. Here's a 12-line script. Save as derive.py; it takes an expression as a string and prints the simplified derivative. python · derive.py 📋 Copy ▶ Run from sympy import symbols, diff, simplify, sympify def derive(expr_str: str, var: str = "x"): x = symbols(var) expr = sympify(expr_str) d = simplify(diff(expr, x)) return d if __name__ == "__main__": print(derive("sin(x**2)")) # → 2*x*cos(x**2) print(derive("ln(cos(x**3))")) # → -3*x**2*tan(x**3) OUTPUT 2*x*cos(x**2) -3*x**2*tan(x**3) That matches what we worked out by hand on both examples. Try plugging in tan(sqrt(x)) next — same recipe, three layers again. 👍 👎 📋 Copy ↻ Try again 📎 🎤 → Try: tan(√x) — derive it Big-O of merge sort Why is i² = −1? Explain Markov chains ⌘↵ to send · model · Atlas-3 ↓ PRACTICE PROBLEMS Chain rule Difficulty · level 2 1 EASY d/dx sin(3x + 2) Solve 💡 Hint Hint · identify the outer and inner functions in sin(3x + 2). Differentiate each separately, then multiply. 2 EASY d/dx (x² + 1)5 Solve 💡 Hint 3 MEDIUM d/dx e^(cos(x)) Solve 💡 Hint 4 MEDIUM d/dx tan(√x) Solve 💡 Hint 5 HARD d/dx ln(sin(x³)) Solve 💡 Hint 6 HARD d/dx (sec(2x))3 Solve 💡 Hint Concepts in this thread Chain rule Calculus · 5 min Derivatives of trig functions Calculus · 3 min Composing functions Pre-calc · 4 min Notation: f', dy/dx, ḟ Calculus · 2 min Your progress Today 4 / 10 problems Streak 14 days · 🔥 Topic mastery Chain rule · 72%

observation.title: Atlas Tutor — math & CS tutor
observation.visible_text: Atlas Tutor + New chat 🔍 SUBJECTS 𝒙 Mathematics 12 {} Programming 7 ⚛ Physics 3 ∮ Statistics 4 ∇ Linear algebra 5 TODAY Chain rule — when both functions move Big-O of recursive Fibonacci L'Hôpital's rule — when can we apply it? LAST 7 DAYS Eigenvalues of a 3 × 3 matrix Bayes' theorem — disease testing Binary search — off-by-one bugs Why does e^x derive to itself? Markov chain steady state EARLIER Proof by induction — sum 1..n Tail recursion vs. loop Series convergence tests cheatsheet Probability of repeat birthdays SA Selene Aiyer Atlas Plus · 14 days streak ⚙ Chain rule — when both functions move Calculus · single variable · last reply 12:08 PT · Atlas-3 model ⌥ Steps ▶ Practice ⋯ SA I keep getting tangled up when I have to differentiate sin(x²). Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! Try this kind of unpacking on the practice problems in the right pane — start with #1. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Can you also write a tiny Python helper that prints the derivative for me using sympy, so I can sanity-check my work? A Sure. Here's a 12-line script. Save as derive.py; it takes an expression as a string and prints the simplified derivative. python · derive.py 📋 Copy ▶ Run from sympy import symbols, diff, simplify, sympify def derive(expr_str: str, var: str = "x"): x = symbols(var) expr = sympify(expr_str) d = simplify(diff(expr, x)) return d if __name__ == "__main__": print(derive("sin(x**2)")) # → 2*x*cos(x**2) print(derive("ln(cos(x**3))")) # → -3*x**2*tan(x**3) OUTPUT 2*x*cos(x**2) -3*x**2*tan(x**3) That matches what we worked out by hand on both examples. Try plugging in tan(sqrt(x)) next — same recipe, three layers again. 👍 👎 📋 Copy ↻ Try again 📎 🎤 → Try: tan(√x) — derive it Big-O of merge sort Why is i² = −1? Explain Markov chains ⌘↵ to send · model · Atlas-3 ↓ PRACTICE PROBLEMS Chain rule Difficulty · level 2 1 EASY d/dx sin(3x + 2) Submit 💡 Hint Hint · identify the outer and inner functions in sin(3x + 2). Differentiate each separately, then multiply. 2 EASY d/dx (x² + 1)5 Submit 💡 Hint 3 MEDIUM d/dx e^(cos(x)) Submit 💡 Hint 4 MEDIUM d/dx tan(√x) Solve 💡 Hint 5 HARD d/dx ln(sin(x³)) Solve 💡 Hint 6 HARD d/dx (sec(2x))3 Solve 💡 Hint Concepts in this thread Chain rule Calculus · 5 min Derivatives of trig functions Calculus · 3 min Composing functions Pre-calc · 4 min Notation: f', dy/dx, ḟ Calculus · 2 min Your progress Today 4 / 10 problems Streak 14 days · 🔥 Topic mastery Chain rule · 72

observation.visible_text: Atlas Tutor + New chat 🔍 SUBJECTS 𝒙 Mathematics 12 {} Programming 7 ⚛ Physics 3 ∮ Statistics 4 ∇ Linear algebra 5 TODAY Chain rule — when both functions move Big-O of recursive Fibonacci L'Hôpital's rule — when can we apply it? Markov chain steady state EARLIER Proof by induction — sum 1..n Tail recursion vs. loop Series convergence tests cheatsheet Probability of repeat birthdays SA Selene Aiyer Atlas Plus · 14 days streak ⚙ Chain rule — when both functions move Calculus · single variable · last reply 12:08 PT · Atlas-3 model ⌥ Steps ▶ Practice ⋯ SA I keep getting tangled up when I have to differentiate sin(x²). Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! Try this kind of unpacking on the practice problems in the right pane — start with #1. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Can you also write a tiny Python helper that prints the derivative for me using sympy, so I can sanity-check my work? A Sure. Here's a 12-line script. Save as derive.py; it takes an expression as a string and prints the simplified derivative. python · derive.py 📋 Copy ▶ Run from sympy import symbols, diff, simplify, sympify def derive(expr_str: str, var: str = "x"): x = symbols(var) expr = sympify(expr_str) d = simplify(diff(expr, x)) return d if __name__ == "__main__": print(derive("sin(x**2)")) # → 2*x*cos(x**2) print(derive("ln(cos(x**3))")) # → -3*x**2*tan(x**3) OUTPUT 2*x*cos(x**2) -3*x**2*tan(x**3) That matches what we worked out by hand on both examples. Try plugging in tan(sqrt(x)) next — same recipe, three layers again. 👍 👎 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Can you explain the chain rule using a real-world analogy? A Got it — I'd start by identifying the layers. For something like Can you explain the chain rule using a real-world analogy?, write out the outer and inner functions, derive each, and stack with the chain rule. Open practice problem #5 on the right and try this same recipe. 📎 🎤 → Try: tan(√x) — derive it Big-O of merge sort Why is i² = −1? LAST 7 DAYS Eigenvalues of a 3 × 3 matrix Bayes' theorem — disease testing Binary search — off-by-one bugs Why does e^x derive to itself? Markov chain steady state EARLIER Proof by induction — sum 1..n Tail recursion vs. loop Series convergence tests cheatsheet Probability of repeat birthdays SA Selene Aiyer Atlas Plus · 14 days streak ⚙ Chain rule — when both functions move Calculus · single variable · last reply 12:08 PT · Atlas-3 model ⌥ Steps ▶ Practice ⋯ SA I keep getting tangled up when I have to differentiate sin(x²). Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! Try this kind of unpacking on the practice problems in the right pane — start with #1. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Can you also write a tiny Python helper that prints the derivative for me using sympy, so I can sanity-check my work? A Sure. Here's a 12-line script. Save as derive.py; it takes an expression as a string and prints the simplified derivative. python · derive.py 📋 Copy ▶ Run from sympy import symbols, diff, simplify, sympify def derive(expr_str: str, var: str = "x"): x = symbols(var) expr = sympify(expr_str) d = simplify(diff(expr, x)) return d if __name__ == "__main__": print(derive("sin(x**2)")) # → 2*x*cos(x**2) print(derive("ln(cos(x**3))")) # → -3*x**2*tan(x**3) OUTPUT 2*x*cos(x**2) -3*x**2*tan(x**3) That matches what we worked out by hand on both examples. Try plugging in tan(sqrt(x)) next — same recipe, three layers again. 👍 👎 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Can you explain the chain rule using a real-world analogy? A Got it — I'd start by identifying the layers. For something like Can you explain the chain rule using a real-world analogy?, write out the outer and inner functions, derive each, and stack with the chain rule. Open practice problem #5 on the right and try this same recipe. 📎 🎤 → Try: tan(√x) — derive it Big-O of merge sort Why is i² = −1? Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! Try this kind of unpacking on the practice problems in the right pane — start with #1. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Can you also write a tiny Python helper that prints the derivative for me using sympy, so I can sanity-check my work? A Sure. Here's a 12-line script. Save as derive.py; it takes an expression as a string and prints the simplified derivative. python · derive.py 📋 Copy ▶ Run from sympy import symbols, diff, simplify, sympify def derive(expr_str: str, var: str = "x"): x = symbols(var) expr = sympify(expr_str) d = simplify(diff(expr, x)) return d if __name__ == "__main__": print(derive("sin(x**2)")) # → 2*x*cos(x**2) print(derive("ln(cos(x**3))")) # → -3*x**2*tan(x**3) OUTPUT 2*x*cos(x**2) -3*x**2*tan(x**3) That matches what we worked out by hand on both examples. Try plugging in tan(sqrt(x)) next — same recipe, three layers again. 👍 👎 📋 Copy ↻ Try again 📎 🎤 → Try: tan(√x) — derive it Big-O of merge sort Why is i² = −1? Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! Try this kind of unpacking on the practice problems in the right pane — start with #1. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Can you also write a tiny Python helper that prints the derivative for me using sympy, so I can sanity-check my work? A Sure. Here's a 12-line script. Save as derive.py; it takes an expression as a string and prints the simplified derivative. python · derive.py 📋 Copy ▶ Run from sympy import symbols, diff, simplify, sympify def derive(expr_str: str, var: str = "x"): x = symbols(var) expr = sympify(expr_str) d = simplify(diff(expr, x)) return d if __name__ == "__main__": print(derive("sin(x**2)")) # → 2*x*cos(x**2) print(derive("ln(cos(x**3))")) # → -3*x**2*tan(x**3) OUTPUT 2*x*cos(x**2) -3*x**2*tan(x**3) That matches what we worked out by hand on both examples. Try plugging in tan(sqrt(x)) next — same recipe, three layers again. 👍 👎 📋 Copy ↻ Try again 📎 🎤 → Try: tan(√x) — derive it Big-O of merge sort Why is i² = −1? Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! Try this kind of unpacking on the practice problems in the right pane — start with #1. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Can you also write a tiny Python helper that prints the derivative for me using sympy, so I can sanity-check my work? A Sure. Here's a 12-line script. Save as derive.py; it takes an expression as a string and prints the simplified derivative. python · derive.py 📋 Copy ▶ Run from sympy import symbols, diff, simplify, sympify def derive(expr_str: str, var: str = "x"): x = symbols(var) expr = sympify(expr_str) d = simplify(diff(expr, x)) return d if __name__ == "__main__": print(derive("sin(x**2)")) # → 2*x*cos(x**2) print(derive("ln(cos(x**3))")) # → -3*x**2*tan(x**3) OUTPUT 2*x*cos(x**2) -3*x**2*tan(x**3) That matches what we worked out by hand on both examples. Try plugging in tan(sqrt(x)) next — same recipe, three layers again. 👍 👎 📋 Copy ↻ Try again 📎 🎤 → Try: tan(√x) — derive it Big-O of merge sort Why is i² = −1? Markov chain steady state EARLIER Proof by induction — sum 1..n Tail recursion vs. loop Series convergence tests cheatsheet Probability of repeat birthdays SA Selene Aiyer Atlas Plus · 14 days streak ⚙ Chain rule — when both functions move Calculus · single variable · last reply 12:08 PT · Atlas-3 model ⌥ Steps ▶ Practice ⋯ SA I keep getting tangled up when I have to differentiate sin(x²). Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! Try this kind of unpacking on the practice problems in the right pane — start with #1. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Can you also write a tiny Python helper that prints the derivative for me using sympy, so I can sanity-check my work? A Sure. Here's a 12-line script. Save as derive.py; it takes an expression as a string and prints the simplified derivative. python · derive.py 📋 Copy ▶ Run from sympy import symbols, diff, simplify, sympify def derive(expr_str: str, var: str = "x"): x = symbols(var) expr = sympify(expr_str) d = simplify(diff(expr, x)) return d if __name__ == "__main__": print(derive("sin(x**2)")) # → 2*x*cos(x**2) print(derive("ln(cos(x**3))")) # → -3*x**2*tan(x**3) OUTPUT 2*x*cos(x**2) -3*x**2*tan(x**3) That matches what we worked out by hand on both examples. Try plugging in tan(sqrt(x)) next — same recipe, three layers again. 👍 👎 📋 Copy ↻ Try again 📎 🎤 → Try: tan(√x) — derive it Big-O of merge sort Why is i² = −1? observation.title: Atlas Tutor — math & CS tutor
observation.visible_text: Atlas Tutor + New chat 🔍 SUBJECTS 𝒙 Mathematics 12 {} Programming 7 ⚛ Physics 3 ∮ Statistics 4 ∇ Linear algebra 5 TODAY Chain rule — when both functions move Big-O of recursive Fibonacci L'Hôpital's rule — when can we apply it? LAST 7 DAYS Eigenvalues of a 3 × 3 matrix Bayes' theorem — disease testing Binary search — off-by-one bugs Why does e^x derive to itself? Markov chain steady state EARLIER Proof by induction — sum 1..n Tail recursion vs. loop Series convergence tests cheatsheet Probability of repeat birthdays SA Selene Aiyer Atlas Plus · 14 days streak ⚙ Chain rule — when both functions move Calculus · single variable · last reply 12:08 PT · Atlas-3 model ⌥ Steps ▶ Practice ⋯ SA I keep getting tangled up when I have to differentiate sin(x²). Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! Try this kind of unpacking on the practice problems in the right pane — start with #1. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Can you also write a tiny Python helper that prints the derivative for me using sympy, so I can sanity-check my work? A Sure. Here's a 12-line script. Save as derive.py; it takes an expression as a string and prints the simplified derivative. python · derive.py 📋 Copy ▶ Run from sympy import symbols, diff, simplify, sympify def derive(expr_str: str, var: str = "x"): x = symbols(var) expr = sympify(expr_str) d = simplify(diff(expr, x)) return d if __name__ == "__main__": print(derive("sin(x**2)")) # → 2*x*cos(x**2) print(derive("ln(cos(x**3))")) # → -3*x**2*tan(x**3) OUTPUT 2*x*cos(x**2) -3*x**2*tan(x**3) That matches what we worked out by hand on both examples. Try plugging in tan(sqrt(x)) next — same recipe, three layers again. 👍 👎 📋 Copy ↻ Try again 📎 🎤 → Try: tan(√x) — derive it Big-O of merge sort Why is i² = −1? Explain Markov chains ⌘↵ to send · model · Atlas-3 ↓ PRACTICE PROBLEMS Chain rule Difficulty · level 2 1 EASY d/dx sin(3x + 2) Solve 💡 Hint 2 EASY d/dx (x² + 1)5 Solve 💡 Hint 3 MEDIUM d/dx e^(cos(x)) Solve 💡 Hint 4 MEDIUM d/dx tan(√x) Solve 💡 Hint 5 HARD d/dx ln(sin(x³)) Solve 💡 Hint 6 HARD d/dx (sec(2x))3 Solve 💡 Hint Concepts in this thread Chain rule Calculus · 5 min Derivatives of trig functions Calculus · 3 min Composing functions Pre-calc · 4 min Notation: f', dy/dx, ḟ Calculus · 2 min Your progress Today 4 / 10 problems Streak 14 days · 🔥 Topic mastery Chain rule · 72%

observation.visible_text: Atlas Tutor + New chat 🔍 SUBJECTS 𝒙 Mathematics 12 {} Programming 7 ⚛ Physics 3 ∮ Statistics 4 ∇ Linear algebra 5 TODAY Chain rule — when both functions move Big-O of recursive Fibonacci L'Hôpital's rule — when can we apply it? Markov chain steady state EARLIER Proof by induction — sum 1..n Tail recursion vs. loop Series convergence tests cheatsheet Probability of repeat birthdays SA Selene Aiyer Atlas Plus · 14 days streak ⚙ Chain rule — when both functions move Calculus · single variable · last reply 12:08 PT · Atlas-3 model ⌥ Steps ▶ Practice ⋯ SA I keep getting tangled up when I have to differentiate sin(x²). Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! Try this kind of unpacking on the practice problems in the right pane — start with #1. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Can you also write a tiny Python helper that prints the derivative for me using sympy, so I can sanity-check my work? A Sure. Here's a 12-line script. Save as derive.py; it takes an expression as a string and prints the simplified derivative. python · derive.py 📋 Copy ▶ Run from sympy import symbols, diff, simplify, sympify def derive(expr_str: str, var: str = "x"): x = symbols(var) expr = sympify(expr_str) d = simplify(diff(expr, x)) return d if __name__ == "__main__": print(derive("sin(x**2)")) # → 2*x*cos(x**2) print(derive("ln(cos(x**3))")) # → -3*x**2*tan(x**3) OUTPUT 2*x*cos(x**2) -3*x**2*tan(x**3) That matches what we worked out by hand on both examples. Try plugging in tan(sqrt(x)) next — same recipe, three layers again. 👍 👎 📋 Copy ↻ Try again 📎 🎤 → Try: tan(√x) — derive it Big-O of merge sort Why is i² = −1? observation.visible_text: Atlas Tutor + New chat 🔍 SUBJECTS 𝒙 Mathematics 12 {} Programming 7 ⚛ Physics 3 ∮ Statistics 4 ∇ Linear algebra 5 TODAY Chain rule — when both functions move Big-O of recursive Fibonacci L'Hôpital's rule — when can we apply it? LAST 7 DAYS Eigenvalues of a 3 × 3 matrix Bayes' theorem — disease testing Binary search — off-by-one bugs Why does e^x derive to itself? Markov chain steady state EARLIER Proof by induction — sum 1..n Tail recursion vs. loop Series convergence tests cheatsheet Probability of repeat birthdays SA Selene Aiyer Atlas Plus · 14 days streak ⚙ Chain rule — when both functions move Calculus · single variable · last reply 12:08 PT · Atlas-3 model ⌥ Steps ▶ Practice ⋯ SA I keep getting tangled up when I have to differentiate sin(x²). Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! Try this kind of unpacking on the practice problems in the right pane — start with #1. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Can you also write a tiny Python helper that prints the derivative for me using sympy, so I can sanity-check my work? A Sure. Here's a 12-line script. Save as derive.py; it takes an expression as a string and prints the simplified derivative. python · derive.py 📋 Copy ▶ Run from sympy import symbols, diff, simplify, sympify def derive(expr_str: str, var: str = "x"): x = symbols(var) expr = sympify(expr_str) d = simplify(diff(expr, x)) return d if __name__ == "__main__": print(derive("sin(x**2)")) # → 2*x*cos(x**2) print(derive("ln(cos(x**3))")) # → -3*x**2*tan(x**3) OUTPUT 2*x*cos(x**2) -3*x**2*tan(x**3) That matches what we worked out by hand on both examples. Try plugging in tan(sqrt(x)) next — same recipe, three layers again. 👍 👎 📋 Copy ↻ Try again 📎 🎤 → Try: tan(√x) — derive it Big-O of merge sort Why is i² = −1? Explain Markov chains ⌘↵ to send · model · Atlas-3 ↓ PRACTICE PROBLEMS Chain rule Difficulty · level 2 1 EASY d/dx sin(3x + 2) Solve 💡 Hint 2 EASY d/dx (x² + 1)5 Solve 💡 Hint 3 MEDIUM d/dx e^(cos(x)) Solve 💡 Hint 4 MEDIUM d/dx tan(√x) Solve 💡 Hint 5 HARD d/dx ln(sin(x³)) Solve 💡 Hint 6 HARD d/dx (sec(2x))3 Solve 💡 Hint Concepts in this thread Chain rule Calculus · 5 min Derivatives of trig functions Calculus · 3 min Composing functions Pre-calc · 4 min Notation: f', dy/dx, ḟ Calculus · 2 min Your progress Today 4 / 10 problems Streak 14 days · 🔥 Topic mastery Chain rule · 72%

Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! Try this kind of unpacking on the practice problems in the right pane — start with #1. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Can you also write a tiny Python helper that prints the derivative for me using sympy, so I can sanity-check my work? Save as derive.py; it takes an expression as a string and prints the simplified derivative. python · derive.py 📋 Copy ▶ Run from sympy import symbols, diff, simplify, sympify def derive(expr_str: str, var: str = "x"): x = symbols(var) expr = sympify(expr_str) d = simplify(diff(expr, x)) return d if __name__ == "__main__": print(derive("sin(x**2)")) # → 2*x*cos(x**2) print(derive("ln(cos(x**3))")) # → -3*x**2*tan(x**3) OUTPUT 2*x*cos(x**2) -3*x**2*tan(x**3) That matches what we worked out by hand on both examples. Markov chain steady state EARLIER Proof by induction — sum 1..n Tail recursion vs. loop Series convergence tests cheatsheet Probability of repeat birthdays SA Selene Aiyer Atlas Plus · 14 days streak ⚙ Chain rule — when both functions move Calculus · single variable · last reply 12:08 PT · Atlas-3 model ⌥ Steps ▶ Practice ⋯ SA I keep getting tangled up when I have to differentiate sin(x²). Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! Try this kind of unpacking on the practice problems in the right pane — start with #1. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Can you also write a tiny Python helper that prints the derivative for me using sympy, so I can sanity-check my work? A Sure. Here's a 12-line script. Save as derive.py; it takes an expression as a string and prints the simplified derivative. python · derive.py 📋 Copy ▶ Run from sympy import symbols, diff, simplify, sympify def derive(expr_str: str, var: str = "x"): x = symbols(var) expr = sympify(expr_str) d = simplify(diff(expr, x)) return d if __name__ == "__main__": print(derive("sin(x**2)")) # → 2*x*cos(x**2) print(derive("ln(cos(x**3))")) # → -3*x**2*tan(x**3) OUTPUT 2*x*cos(x**2) -3*x**2*tan(x**3) That matches what we worked out by hand on both examples. Try plugging in tan(sqrt(x)) next — same recipe, three layers again. 👍 👎 📋 Copy ↻ Try again 📎 🎤 → Try: tan(√x) — derive it Big-O of merge sort Why is i² = −1? observation.visible_text: Chain rule — when both functions move Calculus · single variable · last reply 12:08 PT · Atlas-3 model ⌥ Steps ▶ Practice ⋯ SA I keep getting tangled up when I have to differentiate sin(x²). Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! Try this kind of unpacking on the practice problems in the right pane — start with #1. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Can you also write a tiny Python helper that prints the derivative for me using sympy, so I can sanity-check my work? A Sure. Here's a 12-line script. Save as derive.py; it takes an expression as a string and prints the simplified derivative. python · derive.py 📋 Copy ▶ Run from sympy import symbols, diff, simplify, sympify def derive(expr_str: str, var: str = "x"): x = symbols(var) expr = sympify(expr_str) d = simplify(diff(expr, x)) return d if __name__ == "__main__": print(derive("sin(x**2)")) # → 2*x*cos(x**2) print(derive("ln(cos(x**3))")) # → -3*x**2*tan(x**3) OUTPUT 2*x*cos(x**2) -3*x**2*tan(x**3) That matches what we worked out by hand on both examples. Try plugging in tan(sqrt(x)) next — same recipe, three layers again. 👍 👎 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA What is the derivative of cos(x)? A Got it — I'd start by identifying the layers. For something like What is the derivative of cos(x)?, write out the outer and inner functions, derive each, and stack with the chain rule. Open practice problem #4 on the right and try this same recipe. SA tan(√x) — derive it A Got it — I'd start by identifying the layers. For something like tan(√x) — derive it, write out the outer and inner functions, derive each, and stack with the chain rule. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed.
